Atskuri Jewish Cemetery

Jewish Cemetery · Atskuri, Georgia

Not demolished. Atskuri, an ancient fortress town in Samtskhe-Javakheti, passed through Mongol, Iranian, Ottoman (from 1576), and finally Russian control (from 1829). Oral tradition places Jewish settlement there as early as Queen Tamar's reign (1184-1213); by the 18th century, about 150 Jewish families lived in a dedicated district, trading goods from Asia. A plague during the 1828-29 Russian-Turkish War devastated the population; about 20 more Jewish families arrived from surrounding towns in 1869. Rising Turkish antisemitism and pogroms in the late 19th century drove the community's decline, and the last Jews left Atskuri in 1908 - both local synagogues were later destroyed by the Ottomans. This cemetery is the only surviving Jewish trace in town; though inactive, the Akhaltsikhe Jewish community fenced it in 1957 to prevent disrepair. Its earliest visible tombstone dates to 1906, its latest to 1931; scholar Nisan Babalikashvili documented 1,862 inscriptions there in his research.
